spheres.title: Your phone solves a globe equation several times a second
spheres.mini: Each GPS satellite's signal tells your phone how far away it is, which puts you on a sphere around it. Three spheres, drawn at true scale, meet at one point on the Earth's surface: you.
spheres.text: A GPS receiver measures its distance to each satellite from the signal's travel time, and each distance puts it somewhere on a sphere centred on that satellite. Three range spheres, drawn here at true scale around real orbit positions, meet at a single point on the Earth's surface: the receiver. The satellite positions come from orbital elements the receiver evaluates in Earth-centred coordinates, on the same ellipsoid geodesists use [1]. The fix exists because the geometry is what the broadcast says it is; fed into any other geometry, the ranges fail to meet.
spheres.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: GPS fixes computed in a flat geometry that close as well as the Earth-centred ones.
unknowns.title: Four satellites for four unknowns
unknowns.mini: Each measured range is one equation. The receiver's position has three unknowns, and its cheap clock adds a fourth: its error δt. Four satellites solve all four, which is why a phone chip gets atomic-clock time.
unknowns.text: Each measured range ρᵢ is one equation: ρᵢ = |x − sᵢ(t)| + c·δt, where x is the receiver's position, sᵢ(t) the satellite's broadcast position and δt the receiver clock's error. Three unknowns for the position and one for the clock make four, so four satellites are needed. One microsecond of clock error is 300 m of position error, so solving for δt is what lets a cheap receiver chip use atomic-clock timing [1]. The satellite positions are Earth-centred coordinates on the WGS-84 ellipsoid. The drawing is schematic.
unknowns.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: receivers solving these equations in a flat frame and getting the same fixes.
ranges.title: Each range is a sphere
ranges.mini: A measured range puts you on a sphere around its satellite. Two spheres intersect in a circle, a third cuts it at two points, and the next range decides which one is you.
ranges.text: Written out, each measurement is ρᵢ = √((x − xᵢ)² + (y − yᵢ)² + (z − zᵢ)²) + c·δt: a sphere of known radius around a satellite at a known point in space. Two spheres meet in a circle; a third cuts it at two points, one of them far out in space; the fourth range decides and fixes the clock at the same time. The coordinates are three-dimensional and centred on the Earth's centre of mass. The drawing is schematic.
ranges.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: ranges that meet with the satellites placed over a flat Earth.
sky.title: The GPS constellation, to scale
sky.mini: 24 baseline satellites in six planes tilted 55°, 20,200 km up, each circling twice a day. From anywhere on the sphere, 8 to 12 are above the horizon at once, and the set keeps changing as they rise and set.
sky.text: The constellation at true scale: 24 baseline satellites in six orbital planes inclined 55° [1], 20,200 km up, 4.17 Earth radii from the centre, each circling in 11 h 58 min [2]. From the observer at the latitude named above the text, 8 to 12 satellites are above the horizon at once, highlighted with sight lines, and the set keeps changing as satellites rise and set, as any phone's satellite-status screen shows. A satellite 26,560 km from the centre is above a true horizon for at most 5 h 04 min, from one radius and one orbit. Emitters fixed over a plane would never set.
sky.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: GPS satellites that never set, or that stay above the horizon longer than 5 h 04 min.
clock.title: Why four satellites: closing the clock error
clock.mini: With a perfect clock, three ranges meet at your position. A cheap clock adds the same error to every range and the circles miss. Solving for that error shrinks them until they close: position and time come out together.
clock.text: With a perfect clock, three ranges intersect at the receiver's position. A cheap receiver's clock is off by some unknown δt, which inflates every measured range by the same c·δt: the dashed circles miss each other. Solving for δt alongside the position shrinks them back until they close, and the fix and the exact time come out together. This closure is a strict geometric test, passed millions of times a second everywhere on Earth, and only in the broadcast Earth-centred geometry. The drawing is schematic.
clock.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: ranges that close in a flat geometry without a clock correction.
kepler.title: The orbit's period, from one radius and the Earth's mass
kepler.mini: Kepler's third law with the broadcast orbit radius, 26,560 km, and the Earth's measured gravitational parameter gives a period of 11 h 58 min: exactly the published one. Nothing is left to adjust.
kepler.text: Kepler's third law, T = 2π√(a³/GM), with the broadcast semi-major axis a = 26,560 km and the Earth's measured gravitational parameter GM = 398,600 km³/s², gives T = 11 h 58 min: the published orbital period, to the minute [1]. Half a sidereal day, so each satellite retraces the same ground track daily while the ground slides four minutes eastward beneath it. The constellation's timetable is the equation of motion around a spherical mass, with nothing left to adjust. The drawing is schematic.
kepler.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: satellite periods that do not follow from the orbit radius and the Earth's mass.
relativity.title: Relativity, written into the satellite clocks
relativity.mini: GPS clocks run slow by about 7 μs a day from their speed and fast by about 45 μs a day from sitting higher in the Earth's gravity: a net +38 μs a day. They are built slow on purpose to compensate.
relativity.text: A clock on the ground and a clock in orbit: the two radii set the difference in gravitational potential, and the orbital speed, 3.9 km/s [1], is tangent to the orbit. Speed makes the satellite clocks run slow by about 7 μs a day; sitting higher in the Earth's gravity makes them run fast by about 45 μs a day. The net is +38 μs a day [2], which at 300 m per microsecond would smear positions by about 11 km a day. So the clocks are manufactured slightly slow and tick correctly once in orbit. Both terms come from the Earth's mass and radius. The drawing is schematic.
relativity.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: GPS clocks keeping time without the relativistic offset set by the Earth's mass and radius.
raw-map.title: Real GPS receivers, solved from the raw signals
raw-map.mini: {{grN}} stations around the world, each solved alone from raw GPS pseudoranges, from the origin of the coordinate system: what is left of each range after the fix is {{grRes}} rms.
raw-map.text: On one day, {{grN}} stations of the International GNSS Service recorded the raw pseudoranges of the GPS satellites [1]. Each station is solved alone, every five minutes, from the origin of the coordinates, with four unknowns (x, y, z, receiver clock) from the satellites above 10° [2]; the day's fixes are averaged. What is left of each pseudorange is {{grRes}} rms, 95 % below {{grP95}}: noise, multipath and broadcast-orbit error. Limit: the broadcast orbits are written in the WGS84 frame, so this is a test that can fail, not a measurement from nothing.
raw-map.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: station positions that only solve with kilometre residuals, or that fit a plane better than a sphere.
raw-fit.title: The Earth's radius from receivers that solved themselves
raw-fit.mini: A sphere through {{grN}} stations, each solved alone from its own signals, has R = {{grR}}; the best plane leaves {{grPlane}}. What the sphere leaves is the Earth's flattening: {{grDelta}}.
raw-fit.text: A sphere fitted through the station positions (centre and radius free) has R = {{grR}} (leaving one station out in turn) and its centre {{grCentre}} from the origin of the coordinates [1]. The best plane through the same points leaves {{grPlane}}. The sphere's own {{grSphRms}} rms is the Earth's flattening, not noise: the equator stands {{grDelta}} farther from the centre than the poles, and the WGS84 ellipsoid has {{grWgs}} [2]; remove it and {{grAfter}} remain.
raw-fit.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: a plane fitting better than the sphere.
fx-sphere.title: A sphere through the stations, or a plane
fx-sphere.mini: A sphere of centre c and radius R passes within a few km of stations solved alone from raw signals; a plane cannot, with stations all round the globe.
fx-sphere.text: |x − c| = R is the same as |x|² = 2c·x + (R² − |c|²), linear in c and in R² − |c|²: one least-squares solve over the station positions gives both [1]. A plane would be n·x = d. The drawing is schematic.
fx-sphere.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: stations that lie on a plane.
raw-vis.title: Two stations that do not see the same sky
raw-vis.mini: Two GPS stations {{grAB}} apart track {{grCommon}} satellites in common on average; {{grOnlyA}} are seen only from the first, {{grOnlyB}} only from the second. Nothing here comes from an orbit.
raw-vis.text: One row per satellite, one column per five minutes of the day: blue, tracked only by {{grA}}; purple, only by {{grB}}; teal, by both [1]. The two stations are {{grAB}} apart and never track the same set of satellites. The files say which satellites each receiver tracked, so this uses no orbit and no WGS84 at all.
raw-vis.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: every station seeing the same satellites at the same time.
raw-share.title: No satellite is shared beyond the geometric limit
raw-share.mini: Across {{grPairs}} pairs of stations, the farthest pair that ever tracked the same satellite is {{grShareMax}} apart; the sphere's limit is {{grLimit}}, from two numbers and no free parameter.
raw-share.text: For each of {{grPairs}} pairs of stations, the number of satellites tracked by both at the same time, averaged over the day, against the angle between them [1]. A satellite at a = {{grAEarth}} from the centre [2] can be above the horizon of two points of a sphere of radius R only if they are less than 2·arccos(R/a) apart: {{grLimit}}. The farthest pair that ever shared a satellite is {{grShareMax}} apart, none of the pairs beyond {{grDisjoint}} did. A flat model has a free height for each transmitter and would have to be tuned to land on such a limit.
raw-share.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: pairs of stations that share satellites well beyond that separation.
solve.title: Solve it yourself, from raw GPS signals
solve.mini: {{grN}} stations solved alone from raw pseudoranges ({{grRes}} rms left): a sphere of R = {{grR}} fits, a plane does not, and no satellite is shared beyond {{grShareMax}}, against a geometric limit of {{grLimit}}.
solve.text: On one day, {{grN}} stations of the International GNSS Service recorded raw GPS pseudoranges [1]. Each is solved alone, from the origin of the coordinates, with four unknowns (x, y, z, receiver clock) and the broadcast orbits [2]: {{grRes}} rms is left of each range. A sphere through the stations has R = {{grR}}, the best plane leaves {{grPlane}}; what the sphere leaves is the flattening, {{grDelta}} against {{grWgs}} for WGS84 [3]. Two stations {{grAB}} apart track {{grCommon}} satellites in common, and across {{grPairs}} pairs none is shared beyond {{grShareMax}}; the limit of a sphere is {{grLimit}}, from a = {{grAEarth}} [4]. Limit: the broadcast orbits are in the WGS84 frame, so the first three panels test it rather than measure from nothing; the last two use no orbit.
solve.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: kilometre residuals, a plane fitting better than the sphere, or stations sharing satellites well beyond that separation.
